July 30 (Reuters) - Breaking down what matters today in global energy markets
By Ron Bousso, ROI Energy Columnist
The Middle East conflict is spreading into new ​territory, an unsettling sign that, five months into the war, the standoff between Iran and ‌the United States is becoming ever harder to untangle.
After a brief pause in fighting that began last Saturday, Washington resumed air strikes inside Iran overnight after Tehran launched a salvo of missiles into Jordan. On Wednesday, U.S. and Saudi forces also jointly ​struck Iran-aligned groups in eastern Iraq in response to drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. It ​was the first time Riyadh has openly joined military action alongside Washington.
There was another ⁠dramatic twist the same day. A drone hit a U.S.-owned gas storage tanker at Egypt's Mediterranean port of ​Damietta. Cairo confirmed the incident, although it remains unclear who was behind the attack.
Taken together, the strikes in ​Iraq and Egypt raise the prospect of more countries being pulled into the conflict. That's especially worrying after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement last week announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
There are signs, too, that the Middle East ​conflict could become increasingly intertwined with the war in Ukraine. Last week, Ukrainian drones struck an Iranian commercial ​vessel in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv said was carrying military cargo bound for Russia.
For now, the region appears stuck ‌in an ⁠uneasy middle ground: not a full-scale war, but far from peace. For energy markets, that means living with persistent uncertainty. Concerns about the security and reliability of Gulf oil and gas supplies are no longer seen as a temporary disruption but increasingly as part of the landscape. That may prove to be one of ​the conflict's most lasting ​consequences. More on that in ⁠my latest column.
